name: Koreamaxxing (surgery tourism)

card.summary: Travelling to South Korea for cosmetic surgery and clinic treatments, used by people seeking facial and body changes at competitive prices from highly experienced aesthetic clinics.
card.note: Research on cosmetic surgery abroad documents higher complication and follow-up-care problems; Korea has also had "ghost surgery" cases.

quick.overview:
Koreamaxxing is the looksmaxxing term for going to South Korea to have cosmetic surgery or aesthetic procedures. South Korea has one of the highest per-capita rates of cosmetic surgery in the world, and clinics there are known for eyelid surgery, rhinoplasty and facial contouring. People on looksmaxxing forums describe it as a way to reach hardmaxxing results such as nose tip work or alar base reduction at lower prices than in the West.

The appeal discussed online is price, competition between clinics and routine experience with procedures. Peer-reviewed research looks at cosmetic surgery tourism in general rather than Korea specifically, and documents complications, follow-up difficulty and costs to home health systems.
quick.how: Forum users describe finding clinics through Korean aggregator apps that list procedures and promotional prices, booking consultations (often in advance online or on arrival), and staying in the country through the early recovery period. Some promotional prices come with an obligation to post a before-and-after review. Users typically combine the trip with a stay of one to several weeks.
quick.risks: Reviews of cosmetic surgery tourism report infections, wound problems and revision surgery after returning home, with limited follow-up from the original surgeon. Korea-specific concerns include "ghost surgery", where a substitute operates in place of the named surgeon; security cameras in operating rooms have been mandatory since 2021. Facial contouring such as V-line surgery carries risks including numbness, according to a maxillofacial surgeon cited in coverage.

lead: Koreamaxxing is a term in looksmaxxing communities for travelling to South Korea to obtain plastic surgery or aesthetic treatments in order to improve facial or body appearance. It sits in the "hardmaxxing" category, since it involves surgical procedures such as double eyelid surgery, rhinoplasty and jaw or cheekbone contouring.[1]

South Korea has the highest per-capita rate of elective cosmetic surgery in the world according to ISAPS data cited on Wikipedia, and an industry built around foreign patients: 464,452 medical tourists were reported to have visited for cosmetic surgery in 2018.[1] A looksmax.org guide on the topic argues that Korea is competitively priced and that every operating room is required to have CCTV.[2]

Published research addresses cosmetic surgery tourism broadly. Reviews describe a growing trend and a complication profile that includes infection, with limited follow-up care for patients who return home.[3][4][5]

chain: Obtain surgery such as eyelid, nose or jaw contouring
angle.text: Koreamaxxers use surgery in Korea to change specific facial features, such as eyelid crease, nose tip or jaw width, often citing lower prices and clinic experience. The appearance change comes from the procedure itself, not from the travel.

infobox: Double eyelid surgery, rhinoplasty, facial contouring

paras: Koreamaxxing refers to seeking cosmetic surgery in South Korea, which is widely described as the plastic surgery capital of the world.[1] It is usually discussed by people already considering surgical changes, including non-Asian users who ask whether Korea is a viable destination.[2]

A looksmax.org guide author writes that non-Asians are hesitant to go but that it is "not that big of a deal", that prices are low because of competition and currency, and that clinics can be found through an app called Gangnam Unni.[2]

sections.h: Background: cosmetic surgery in South Korea
paras: Wikipedia reports that around one in five Korean women had undergone plastic surgery by 2012 and that self-reported surgery among women rose sharply between the mid-1990s and 2015. It links the trend to social pressure around employment and marriage, the influence of K-pop idols, and older physiognomy traditions.[1]
Popular procedures include double eyelid surgery, rhinoplasty and facial contouring such as V-line surgery, which can involve jaw wiring and swelling lasting up to six months.[1]

Users on forums describe browsing clinic listings, comparing promotional prices, and arranging consultations. Some event prices come with a requirement to post a review with before-and-after photos, which can often be blurred.[2] Recovery is typically spent in the country.
Forum members mention procedures such as tip plasty and alar base reduction as reasons to consider Korea.[2]

No studies have examined "koreamaxxing" as such. Research on cosmetic surgery tourism in general includes a Journal of Travel Medicine review of the scale of the practice and its complication profile,[3] a legal review noting regulatory and liability gaps,[4] and surveys and cost analyses of patients returning to the US, UK and Ireland with complications after surgery abroad.[6][7][8] A systematic review of breast surgery tourism found the evidence base consists largely of retrospective case series.[5] Reviews describe infections, including atypical mycobacterial infection after implant surgery, in returning patients.[9]
Reviews of surgery abroad cite limited preoperative counselling, non-specialist operators in some destinations, and difficulties with follow-up care and revision.[3][6]

In South Korea, "ghost surgery", in which an unlicensed substitute operates while the hired surgeon is absent, has been reported; the Korean Society of Plastic Surgeons estimated about 100,000 victims from 2008 to 2014, according to Wikipedia. Lawmakers mandated operating-room cameras in August 2021.[1] V-line surgery carries risks of permanent numbness, according to a surgeon cited there.[1]

timeline.event: American surgeons introduce plastic surgery techniques during the Korean War, per Wikipedia.[1]
Asian financial crisis; labour market changes increase pressure to improve job prospects through appearance.[1]
464,452 foreign medical tourists reported for cosmetic surgery in Korea.[1]

lore.intro: Koreamaxxing appears on looksmax.org mainly as advice threads from members who have had or are planning surgery there.[2]

claims.claim: Korea offers lower prices and safer clinics than other surgery destinations
claims.believers: A forum guide says Korean prices are low due to competition and a weak currency, and that mandatory CCTV in operating rooms limits misconduct.[2]
claims.experts: Reviews of cosmetic surgery tourism report complications and follow-up problems across destinations, and Korea has its own ghost-surgery reports.[3][1]

claims.claim: Non-Asians can travel to Korea for surgery easily
claims.believers: The guide author says it is not a big deal for non-Asians and lists apps for finding clinics.[2]
claims.experts: No studies compare outcomes for foreign patients in Korea specifically.
